title: Git & GitHub
objectives: Understand Git via a real-life analogy
Model repositories, branches, commits, HEAD, remotes
Handle rebase, merge, cherry-pick, stash, reflog like a senior
Recover from mistakes safely (never lose work)
Manage GitHub PRs + reviews + collaboration norms

sections.markdown:
**Think of Git as a time machine for your project + a photocopier for parallel realities.**

Every commit is a snapshot of the whole tree (not a diff — a full state, deduplicated via content addressing). Every branch is a movable pointer into that snapshot history. HEAD is 'you are here.' Merging is joining two histories. Rebasing is replaying commits on a different base.

- **Distributed** — every clone has the full history; no single point of failure.
- **Content-addressed** — every object (blob, tree, commit) has a SHA-1 hash of its content; identical content = identical hash = zero duplication.
- **Immutable** — you don't 'edit' a commit; you make a new one that supersedes.
- **Cheap branches** — a branch is just a 40-char file pointing to a commit.
- **GitHub adds** — hosted remote, PRs, code review UI, Actions CI, issue tracking, releases.

**Why every serious Flutter dev must own Git deeply:** small mistakes compound (rebase gone wrong, force-push over teammate's work); confident senior engineers make the same operations reversible via reflog + stash + backup branches. The devs who ship fast + safely all speak fluent Git.

**Git** is a distributed version control system by Linus Torvalds (2005). Object model: **blobs** (file contents), **trees** (directory structures), **commits** (tree + parents + author + message), **tags** (named pointers). References: **branches** (movable pointers), **HEAD** (current position), **remotes** (URLs to other repos). GitHub is a hosted remote + collaboration surface — PRs, issues, Actions, releases.
## Command essentials

rows: Copy a commit onto current branch

sections.markdown: ## Daily flow — feature branch → PR → merge

sections.code:
# 1. Sync base
git switch main
git pull

# 2. Branch
git switch -c feature/add-scanner

# 3. Work + commit
git add lib/scanner.dart
git commit -m "scanner: initial mobile_scanner integration"

# 4. Push
git push -u origin feature/add-scanner

# 5. Open PR on GitHub
gh pr create --title "Add barcode scanner" --body "…"

# 6. Address review comments → new commits (don't force-push during review)

# 7. Before merge, rebase onto latest main
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# resolve conflicts if any → git add → git rebase --continue
git push --force-with-lease

# 8. Merge via GitHub — squash-and-merge is common convention

# 9. Clean up
git switch main && git pull
git branch -d feature/add-scanner

sections.markdown: ## Recovery — reflog is your safety net

sections.code:
# Accidentally reset --hard? Not lost!
git reflog                          # every HEAD movement in last 90 days
git reset --hard HEAD@{4}            # go back to 4 movements ago

# Force-pushed over teammate's work? Fetch + reset to the pre-push commit.
git fetch
git log --all --oneline               # find the sha before your force-push
git reset --hard <sha>
git push --force-with-lease           # ONLY after coordinating

# Untracked / staged changes gone? — those aren't in reflog. Prevent with:
git stash push -u -m "before risky op"

sections.markdown: ## Common mistakes
**Mistake 1: `git push --force` on shared branch.** Overwrites remote history + drops teammates' commits. Use `--force-with-lease` — fails if remote moved.
**Mistake 2: Rebase after the branch is shared with reviewers.** Reviewers lose their in-progress comments + review UI breaks. Rebase before push OR use fixup commits + squash at merge.
**Mistake 3: `git commit --amend` after push.** Local sha diverges from remote; next push fails or needs force. Amend only pre-push.
**Mistake 4: `git reset --hard` without stashing.** Uncommitted work is GONE (not in reflog). Stash first, always.
**Mistake 5: Committing secrets.** API keys, service-account JSON, `.env` in git → grepable forever. Use `.gitignore` + secret scanning + rotate keys immediately if leaked.
**Mistake 6: Huge binary files.** Git stores them forever; repo becomes 10 GB. Use Git LFS for large assets.
**Mistake 7: Merge conflicts resolved wrong (keeping only 'ours').** Silent bug intro. Read the conflict carefully + test after resolve.
**Mistake 8: Not signing commits.** GPG / SSH signing verifies author; SOC 2 / enterprise environments require it.
## Best practices
**1. Small focused commits** — one logical change each.
**2. Commit-message convention** — Conventional Commits: `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `chore:`, `test:`. Auto-generates changelogs.
**3. Feature branches + PRs** — never commit directly to main.
**4. `--force-with-lease` never `--force`.**
**5. Stash before risky ops.**
**6. Signed commits** (GPG/SSH).
**7. `.gitignore` early** + secret scanning.
**8. `gh` CLI** for PRs from terminal.
## Practice programs
**Practice 1 (Easy)** — Init a repo + first commit + push to GitHub.
**Practice 2 (Medium)** — Feature branch → rebase onto main → PR → squash-merge.
**Practice 3 (Medium)** — Interactive rebase to reorder + squash + edit commits.
**Practice 4 (Hard)** — Recover from an accidental `git reset --hard` via reflog.
**Practice 5 (Hard)** — Bisect: find a bug's introducing commit.
**Practice 6 (Expert)** — Cross-fork PR + reviewer flow via `gh pr` + auto-merge.
## Interview Q&A

**Q1: Merge vs rebase — trade-offs?**

**A:** **Merge** creates a merge commit joining two histories; preserves the exact chronological + branching structure. **Pros:** truth-preserving, safe (no history rewrite), easy to revert. **Cons:** noisy history with merge commits; `git log --graph` can look tangled. **Rebase** replays your commits ON TOP of the new base, producing a linear history. **Pros:** clean linear log, easier `git bisect`, no merge-commit noise. **Cons:** rewrites history (bad if shared); can lose review context; conflicts must be resolved per commit. **Rule:** rebase BEFORE pushing (private history) → clean; merge AFTER pushing (shared history) → safe. GitHub's **squash-and-merge** is a hybrid: local rebase during dev, single squash-commit into main. Most teams use squash-and-merge as the default. Interviewer signal: knowing when each fits.

**Q2: You've `git reset --hard` and lost work — what do you do?**

**A:** **First rule: DON'T PANIC + DON'T do more operations.** Run `git reflog` — every HEAD movement in the last 90 days (config) is logged. Find the sha before the reset (`HEAD@{2}` or similar). Restore: `git reset --hard HEAD@{2}` OR `git branch recovery <sha>` (safer — creates a branch pointing at the lost state). **Caveat:** only tracked + committed work is in reflog. **Untracked** files are gone. **Uncommitted staged/unstaged** changes may still be in `git fsck --lost-found` (dangling blobs) but recovery is painful. **Prevention:** `git stash push -u -m 'safety'` BEFORE any risky op. **The reflog is a superpower** — knowing it exists separates senior from junior devs.

**Q3: When would you use cherry-pick vs merge vs rebase?**

**A:** **`git cherry-pick`** — replay ONE specific commit onto the current branch. Use for: hot-fix backport (fix committed to main → cherry-pick onto release/1.0 branch); porting a specific improvement across branches; recovering a lost commit by SHA. **Merge** — combine an ENTIRE history from another branch. Use for: feature-branch → main integration; long-lived branch consolidation. **Rebase** — replay a SEQUENCE of your commits onto a new base. Use for: catching your feature branch up to main; cleaning up local history before push. **Cherry-pick creates duplicates** — the same logical change lives on two branches with different SHAs; be aware for `git log` reads. Interviewer bonus: knowing that `git rebase --onto` is basically a batched cherry-pick.

**Q4: How does GitHub PR review work + what makes a good PR?**

**A:** **PR anatomy:** source branch + target branch + description + reviewers + status checks (CI, code coverage, security scans). **Reviewer flow:** view diff → leave inline comments → suggest changes → approve / request changes. **Good PR practices:** (1) **Small, focused** — <400 LOC ideal; huge PRs get rubber-stamped. (2) **Clear description** — what, why, how to test, screenshots for UI changes. (3) **Green CI** before requesting review. (4) **Address every comment** with reply or fixup commit. (5) **Rebase onto latest main** before merge. (6) **Follow conventional commit format** for the merge commit. (7) **Update CHANGELOG + docs** if user-facing. (8) **Draft PRs** for early feedback. **Bad PR:** 3K lines + 'refactor' description + no tests → reviewers demoralized. Interviewer signal: 'good PR' is a culture indicator.

**Q5: How do you handle secrets that accidentally leaked into git history?**

**A:** **Assume the secret is compromised the moment it lands on GitHub.** Steps: (1) **Rotate the secret IMMEDIATELY** — new API key, new service account, whatever. Old key is dead. (2) **Do NOT try to `git rm` + push** — the leaked commit is still in the remote's git history + accessible via SHA. (3) **Rewrite history** via `git filter-repo` (modern) or `BFG` (older) to remove the secret from all commits; force-push. (4) **Coordinate with team** — everyone must re-clone or reset because their clones still have the leak. (5) **Enable secret scanning** — GitHub built-in, git-secrets, TruffleHog. (6) **Post-mortem** — how did it land in git? add hooks / CI checks to prevent. (7) **Audit access logs** — did anyone besides your team fetch the leak? **Interviewer signal:** knowing rotation-first is the correct instinct.

**Q6: What are Git hooks + how would you use them?**

**A:** **Git hooks** are shell scripts in `.git/hooks/` that fire on Git events. **Client-side:** `pre-commit` (lint, format check, secret scan), `commit-msg` (enforce commit message format), `pre-push` (run tests). **Server-side:** `pre-receive`, `update`, `post-receive` (enforce policies on the remote). **Tooling:** `pre-commit` framework (Python) or `husky` (Node) manages hooks portably across the team via a config file. **Flutter examples:** pre-commit runs `dart format` + `flutter analyze`; commit-msg enforces Conventional Commits; pre-push runs `flutter test`. **Server-side on GitHub:** GitHub Actions or Branch Protection Rules replace server hooks. **Trap:** hooks live in `.git/` = not versioned; use husky / pre-commit to share via the repo. Interviewer bonus signal.

## Real-world usage

- **Every professional Flutter project** — feature branches + PRs + squash-merge.
- **Release branches** — long-lived for hotfixes.
- **Monorepos** — Melos or Nx to coordinate multi-package repos.
- **CI integration** — GitHub Actions triggered on PR + push.
- **NOT ideal for** — massive binary asset repos (Git LFS or artifact storage).

## Advanced notes

- **`git worktree`** — multiple branches checked out simultaneously in different directories.
- **`git bisect`** — binary-search for a bug's introducing commit.
- **`git blame`** — see who last touched each line.
- **`git switch` vs `git checkout`** — modern replacement for common checkout tasks.
- **`git restore`** vs `git reset` — modern granular API.
- **`git sparse-checkout`** — partial-clone of monorepo.
- **Signed commits** — GPG or SSH keys; SOC 2 requirement.
- **`gh` CLI** — GitHub from terminal.
- **`.gitattributes`** — line-ending + diff behavior per file type.
- **Submodules vs subtrees** — for embedded dependencies; submodules are fragile.
- **Git LFS** — external storage for big files.
- **CODEOWNERS** — auto-assign reviewers.
- **Branch protection rules** — require checks + reviews before merge.
- **PR templates + issue templates** — enforce structure.
- **Squash-merge vs rebase-merge vs merge-commit** — team convention.
- **`git filter-repo`** — history rewriting (replaces `git filter-branch`).
